Centre questions Karnataka’s Ethanol testing process. So what is the prescribed procedure

The Centre has found fault with Karnataka’s sampling and testing methods used to claim that petrol contained 26-31 percent ethanol. ThePrint explains how ethanol content is supposed to be tested.

Udit Bubna

10 November, 2026 09:30 am IST

Follow Us:

-->

Facebook

X

LinkedIn

WhatsApp

Email

Copy Link

Representational image | Reuters

Stay updated with ThePrint:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

-->

New Delhi: India’s E20 programme requires oil marketing companies to ensure that petrol supplied to consumers meets prescribed ethanol-blending and fuel-quality standards, with ethanol content maintained within the 19–21 percent range. But verifying whether the fuel meets these standards depends not just on the laboratory conducting the test, but also on how samples are collected, handled and analysed.

Oil marketing companies (OMCs) allege that Karnataka’s October exercise deviated from the prescribed procedure. They say samples were collected without their representatives present and that they have not received the retained samples, outlet-wise details or laboratory reports.

These procedures have come under scrutiny following Karnataka’s Congress government claiming that petrol sold at certain retail outlets in the state contained 26–31 percent ethanol, significantly above the prescribed E20 limit of 20 percent ethanol.

Show Full Article

The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas (MoPNG) and the three public sector OMCs—Indian Oil Corporation Limited (IOCL), Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL) and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL)—have questioned both the sampling process and the laboratory methods used in Karnataka’s October 2026 exercise.

The latest controversy comes amid wider concerns over E20 petrol. In July, the policy faced criticism over possible mileage losses, particularly in older vehicles. The Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM) also flagged fuel-quality concerns, including chloride contamination and moisture, in a communication to the petroleum ministry. It later withdrew the communication, saying some figures needed further authentication.

EXPOSED: The document the Government tried hard to erase.

On July 28, 2026, SIAM officially warned the Union Govt that Excessive chloride in E20 petrol is actively damaging your vehicles.

Instead of protecting your hard earned money & your vehicles the govt went after news… pic.twitter.com/UEvExxS2jT

— Tehseen Poonawalla Official 🇮🇳 (@tehseenp) August 11, 2026

While the July debate centred on mileage and vehicle compatibility, the Karnataka controversy concerns whether petrol contained more ethanol than permitted. The process requires petrol samples to be collected and analysed in accordance with prescribed procedures.

According to Centre, these procedures are laid down under the Motor Spirit and High-Speed Diesel (Regulation of Supply, Distribution and Prevention of Malpractices) Order, 2005, issued under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, and the Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG) 2024.

Under these rules, six one-litre samples must be collected from a petrol outlet. Two are handed to the dealer against acknowledgement, two are retained by the oil company or inspecting department, and the remaining two are sent to a laboratory specified under the control order.

Sample labels must be jointly signed, and test results communicated to the dealer and oil company within the prescribed timeframe. This allows all parties to verify the findings and seek retesting if they disagree.

The OMCs have also questioned the use of certificates from a third-party laboratory instead of a laboratory specified under the control order. The OMCs say the absence of samples and documentation has prevented them and the dealers from independently verifying the results or seeking a retest.

What methods should laboratories use? Even if samples are collected correctly, laboratories must follow prescribed technical standards to establish their ethanol content.

The relevant specification is identified under IS 17021:2018, the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) standard for ethanol-blended motor gasoline. The amendment, issued in August 2025, prescribes three methods for measuring ethanol content in E20 petrol.

The first is Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), which uses infrared light to identify and measure the concentration of substances in a fuel sample.

The second is water extraction method. Since ethanol mixes readily with water while petrol does not, this method uses water to separate ethanol from petrol before measuring its content through the prescribed procedure.

The third is Gas Chromatography, a laboratory technique that separates the different chemical components of a fuel sample so their individual quantities can be measured. It must follow the prescribed ASTM D4815 or D6839 standards. ASTM International is an organisation that develops standardised testing methods for materials and products.

Gas Chromatography also has specific requirements. The sample must first be diluted in equal proportions with oxygenate-free petrol, meaning petrol without ethanol or other oxygen-containing blending components. The result must then be corrected using an E10 certified reference material—a sample with a known composition used to check the accuracy of laboratory measurements.

The Centre says Karnataka’s laboratory certificates only mention that ethanol was measured using Gas Chromatography. They do not specify which ASTM standard was followed, whether the required dilution was carried out or which reference material was used.

Without these details, the reported ethanol levels of 26–31 percent cannot be independently validated against IS 17021, the Centre argues.

Why the Centre questioned the results The Ministry has questioned the density readings in Karnataka’s certificates. Since ethanol is denser than petrol, a higher ethanol proportion would ordinarily be expected to increase the fuel’s overall density.

Karnataka’s certificates recorded densities of 0.742–0.749 grams per cubic centimetre for samples reportedly containing 26-31 percent ethanol. In comparison, OMC tests of E20 samples recorded densities of 0.752–0.760 grams per cubic centimetre. The Centre says this difference warrants further examination through prescribed testing and comparison with appropriate reference samples.

The OMCs have also cited their nationwide quality-monitoring exercise conducted with the Centre for High Technology (CHT), under Petroleum Ministry. Of 893 samples collected from depots and retail outlets across 27 states and Union Territories, all were found to contain ethanol within the prescribed range of 19-21 percent.

This included 56 samples from Karnataka, covering all three OMCs and different locations. Their ethanol content ranged between 19 and 20 percent, averaging 19.30 percent.

The OMCs have sought Karnataka’s sampling records, laboratory reports and access to the samples. They have proposed joint testing at an authorised laboratory with representatives of both sides to establish whether the reported ethanol levels are accurate and meet the prescribed testing standards.

(Edited by Viny Mishra)

バンナムＨＤ、今期純利益1620億円に上方修正　トイホビー好調 12:37 配信

年次ゲーム見本市「E3」のバンダイナムコＨＤのブース。2019年6月11日、米国カリフォルニア州ロサンゼルスで撮影。REUTERS/Mike Blake（ロイター） [東京 １０日 ロイター] - バンダイナムコホールディングスは１０日、２０２７年３月期の純利益予想を１３００億円から１６２０億円（前年比１５．２％増）に上方修正すると発表した。「ガンダム」関連商品などを手掛けるトイホビー事業がけん引し、４─９月期の業績が予想を大幅に上回ったことが主因。

・ＩＢＥＳがまとめたアナリスト１９人の予測平均値は１５９５億円

・営業利益予想も１８５０億円から２２６０億円に引き上げ

・トイホビー事業の４─９月期利益は５５．４％増。「ガンダム」シリー ズのプラモデルやカプセル入りおもちゃ、「ドラゴンボール」や「たまごっち」などのＩＰ（知的財産）展開が好調。

・４─９月期純利益は前年比２６．１％増の約９９５億円

・カナダ子会社の解散に伴い、第３・四半期以降に約３５億円の特別損失を計上見込み

item.title: Japan's Nikkei surges nearly 3% as AI stks extend rebound
item.description: Japan's Nikkei index jumped nearly 3% on Tuesday as AI and semiconductor stocks recovered from Friday's sharp selloff. SoftBank Group surged over 14%, leading the tech-driven rally alongside chip equipment makers, despite overnight losses in Nvidia shares and cautious sentiment near key resistance levels.
item.dc:creator: Anupam Nagar
item.content:encoded: Japan's Nikkei share average climbed nearly 3% on Tuesday, extending its recovery from a sharp technology-led selloff last week as artificial intelligence-related stocks staged a strong rebound, Reuters reported.The Nikkei rose 2.88% to 60,471.05 by 0158 GMT, recovering most of the losses suffered during Friday's steep decline over the past two trading sessions. The broader Topix index advanced 2.27% to 3,904.67.The rebound followed a nearly 6% slump in the Nikkei on Friday, when AI-related stocks came under heavy selling pressure amid concerns that the US Congress could slow investment in artificial intelligence following the Democrats' decisive victory in the midterm elections.Read more: Global Market Today: Asian stocks rally after US tech surge, oil slumpAccording to Reuters, the latest gains were driven by renewed buying in technology and semiconductor stocks, although investors remained cautious about the possibility of the Nikkei crossing the 61,000 mark.Technology investor SoftBank Group surged 14.38% on Tuesday, while semiconductor equipment makers Advantest and Tokyo Electron gained 4.93% and 5.66%, respectively. Memory-chip maker Kioxia jumped 7.6%.The gains came despite Nvidia shares falling 4.2% overnight amid controversy surrounding its CEO Jensen Huang. However, investors appeared to view the developments as largely company-specific rather than a broader threat to the artificial intelligence industry, Reuters reported.Read more: US stocks: Dow rockets 1,100 points, S&P over 2% as oil slide cools inflation worries; Nvidia slumpsKioxia's rally also came as some investors unwound leveraged positions following Friday's selloff to avoid margin calls. Outstanding margin-buying positions in the stock declined to 48.22 million shares from 52.85 million a day earlier, according to Tokyo Stock Exchange data.Kioxia accounts for a significant portion of outstanding margin-buying positions after emerging as a major contributor to the Nikkei's rally to a record high in June. The stock has subsequently faced pressure amid deteriorating sentiment towards AI-related shares.Elsewhere, JX Advanced Metals rose 2.2% after the semiconductor materials maker raised its net profit forecast for the financial year ending next March by 14%.However, gains across the broader market were not uniform. Toyota Motor fell 1.63%, making it the biggest drag on the Topix, while soy sauce maker Kikkoman plunged 13% to become the biggest percentage loser on the Nikkei.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

item.title: China’s Trade Surplus Tops $1 Trillion as October Exports Surge
item.description: China’s trade surplus surged past $1 trillion in the first 10 months as a global race to build AI infrastructure buoyed sales of high-tech products and helped offset weak domestic demand, a dynamic likely to sharpen tensions with major trading partners. The figures highlight Beijing’s …
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded:
China’s trade surplus surged past $1 trillion in the first 10 months as a global race to build AI infrastructure buoyed sales of high-tech products and helped offset weak domestic demand, a dynamic likely to sharpen tensions with major trading partners.

The figures highlight Beijing’s growing reliance on overseas demand to support an economy hobbled by subdued consumption and a protracted property slump. But while the global AI investment boom is expected to keep demand for Chinese technology products strong into 2027, it risks deepening domestic imbalances and fuelling trade frictions with partners including the European Union.

Exports rose sharply by 35.2% in October from the same month last year in US dollar terms, customs data showed Tuesday, only a touch slower than the 36.3% surge in September but ahead of economists’ forecast for a 33.5% increase.

That helped lift China’s trade surplus to $1.04 trillion in the first 10 months, topping $1 trillion for a second consecutive year and reaching the milestone a month earlier than in 2025.

The swelling surplus could fuel further tensions with the European Union, where leaders have called for more trade curbs with China after reaching an agreement with Beijing to limit Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc over the next few years. Because the measures have yet to take effect, factories are expected to bring forward shipments, bolstering exports in the near term.

China on Monday officially announced the extension of a trade truce with Washington due to expire on November 10 by two months, but said last week that expanding its purchases of US farm goods would hinge on the implementation of their agreed reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement.

“The risk of additional tariffs and other trade barriers will remain elevated in 2027, particularly as Chinese manufacturers continue expanding their presence in overseas markets,” said Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at Trivium China.

Imports grew 41.6%, beating the median forecast for a 32% increase in the Reuters poll and accelerating from the 31% growth in September.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit will take place next week in the southern Chinese tech and innovation hub Shenzhen, where Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are expected to meet for the third time so far this year.

Headwinds and Uncertainties

One big worry for Beijing is that consumers remain reluctant to spend, constrained by a property market downturn that has battered household wealth and dented confidence in the economic outlook.

Sluggish demand at home has pushed Chinese automakers to seek sales in overseas markets. China’s car exports maintained a solid pace of growth in October, while domestic vehicle sales recorded a 12th straight month of declines, separate data released by an industry association showed.

Greater reliance on exports, however, leaves China’s economy increasingly exposed to any slowdown in global demand.

Much of the strength in exports this year has been fuelled by a global push to expand AI infrastructure.

“The outlook for exports depends on how long the AI boom will last,” Macquarie analysts wrote. They expect China’s exports to accelerate further in the fourth quarter before starting to slow from the first quarter of 2027.

item.title: Higher financing costs to weaken global credit conditions in 2027: Moody's
item.description: Moody's Ratings expects global credit conditions to weaken in 2027 as higher financing costs and energy prices strain borrowers, while AI investments and policy shifts reshape markets ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Higher financing costs to weaken global credit conditions in 2027: Moody's

Higher financing costs to weaken global credit conditions in 2027: Moody's Moody's Ratings expects global credit conditions to weaken in 2027 as higher financing costs and energy prices strain borrowers, while AI investments and policy shifts reshape markets

(Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India New Delhi 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 10 2026 | 4:36 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Moody's Ratings on Tuesday said it expects global credit conditions to weaken in 2027 due to higher financing costs and elevated energy prices. The Moody's Ratings' 2027 Global Credit Conditions Outlook report examines the key forces that could shape credit markets in the year ahead. It said AI investment will remain massive, but investors will increasingly focus on whether revenues and productivity gains justify the scale of spending. "Business model disruption will become more visible: some companies will gain from stronger demand and productivity, while others face more competition and weaker pricing power," Moody's Ratings said. Besides, Moody's expects government intervention through tariffs, regulation, export controls and strategic investment to play a growing role in credit outcomes.

"As many of these tools can be introduced or reversed by executive action, policy can shift quickly, therefore this will continue to influence trade, capital allocation and competition in 2027," it added. Rising spending on energy security, critical minerals, defence, and climate resilience will create opportunities for some sectors while increasing costs for others. Also, higher refinancing costs will put greater pressure on highly leveraged issuers and borrowers with significant near-term maturities. "Moody's Ratings expects global credit conditions to weaken in 2027 as higher financing costs and elevated energy prices create pockets of pressure, even as major economies continue to expand," the agency said.

item.title: Three workers die at Tata Electronics' Hosur plant; Nalco Water confirms incident at utility facility
item.description: Nalco Water, an Ecolab company, on Tuesday confirmed that three workers employed by its subcontractor died in an incident at Tata Electronics' iPhone components manufacturing facility in Hosur, Tamil ...
item.content:encoded:
Three workers die at Tata Electronics' Hosur plant; Nalco Water confirms incident at utility facility Nalco Water, an Ecolab company, on Tuesday confirmed that three workers employed by its subcontractor died in an incident at Tata Electronics' iPhone components manufacturing facility in Hosur, Tamil Nadu, and said it was cooperating with local authorities investigating the deaths. ANI | Updated: 10-11-2026 16:11 IST | Created: 10-11-2026 16:11 IST

A security guard stands at the boundary of a Tata Electronics' components factory for Apple’s iPhone in Hosur, Tamil Nadu, India (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Nalco Water, an Ecolab company, on Tuesday confirmed that three workers employed by its subcontractor died in an incident at Tata Electronics' iPhone components manufacturing facility in Hosur, Tamil Nadu, and said it was cooperating with local authorities investigating the deaths. The company said the incident occurred at a utility facility operated by Nalco Water. "We are deeply saddened by the tragic incident that resulted in the deaths of three workers engaged by a sub-contractor of Nalco Water, an Ecolab company, at the Tata Electronics site in Hosur, India," the company said in a statement. "This incident occurred in a utility facility, operated by Nalco Water. We are working with the local authorities in the investigation of this incident," it added. The three workers died on Monday evening while carrying out maintenance work at an effluent treatment plant at Tata Electronics' Hosur facility, which manufactures components for Apple's iPhones. According to local authorities, the workers inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank at the wastewater treatment facility. They were subsequently taken to a hospital, where they were declared dead, reported Reuters. Nalco Water said its immediate priority was to support the families of the deceased workers. "We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those impacted. Our thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected and our first priority is to extend all possible support to the families," the company said. Reiterating its commitment to workplace safety, Ecolab said, "Safety is a core value and is fundamental to everything we do at Ecolab. We take this incident extremely seriously." The deaths come amid growing scrutiny of Apple's manufacturing supply chain in India, which has emerged as a major production hub as the US technology company diversifies operations beyond China. India currently accounts for roughly 25 per cent of global iPhone production, with Tata Electronics contributing about 40 per cent of iPhone assembly in the country. Tata's Hosur operations have faced disruptions in the past, including a fire at its components factory in September 2024 that halted production. The facility also faced regulatory concerns over alleged water pollution earlier this year, although the matter was subsequently resolved. Separately, a ransomware attack affected an adjacent Tata Electronics iPhone manufacturing facility in Hosur earlier this year, exposing confidential company documents. (ANI)

FAST

TOKYO, Nov 10 : The Bank of Japan estimates that its accelerated sales of exchange-traded fund (ETF) holdings will generate about 1 trillion yen ($6.33 billion) in additional annual proceeds, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Tuesday. Katayama's remarks come after Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi unveiled plans last week to tap proceeds from the BOJ's ETF sales to fund investment in areas deemed vital to Japan's economic security, as the government seeks new revenue sources without relying excessively on debt issuance. The BOJ decided on October 30 to increase annual sales of its ETF holdings to 860 billion yen from 330 billion yen on a book-value basis. A portion of net profit the central bank reaps each year, including from the ETF sales, is paid to state coffers. "The BOJ has indicated additional proceeds of roughly 1 trillion yen, but the exact amount that will be remitted to the government will depend on fiscal year-end calculations and budget procedures, so we can't say precisely how much it will be," Katayama said.

item.title: China’s new Anti-Corruption law raises fears of legalising transnational repression, analysts say
item.description: China's newly enacted Anti-Cross-Border Corruption Law has raised concerns that Beijing could use anti-corruption measures to legitimise its overseas operations against dissidents and political ...
item.content:encoded:
China’s new Anti-Corruption law raises fears of legalising transnational repression, analysts say China's newly enacted Anti-Cross-Border Corruption Law has raised concerns that Beijing could use anti-corruption measures to legitimise its overseas operations against dissidents and political opponents, creating a chilling effect on critics of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), according to a report by The Epoch Times. ANI | Updated: 10-11-2026 15:58 IST | Created: 10-11-2026 15:58 IST

Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

China's newly enacted Anti-Cross-Border Corruption Law has raised concerns that Beijing could use anti-corruption measures to legitimise its overseas operations against dissidents and political opponents, creating a chilling effect on critics of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), according to a report by The Epoch Times. The Standing Committee of China's National People's Congress (NPC) adopted the legislation on November 6, following the CCP's Fifth Plenum, which focused on advancing what the party described as "full and rigorous governance of the party" amid an expanding internal disciplinary campaign, The Epoch Times reported. According to the Chinese regime, the law formalises and consolidates operations by state agencies to track down and bring back Chinese nationals suspected of corruption who have fled overseas, while also enabling the confiscation of allegedly illegally acquired assets across international borders. However, analysts cited by The Epoch Times warned that the legislation could provide Beijing with a legal framework to expand its reach beyond China's borders and intensify pressure on overseas dissidents. Wang He, a US-based senior analyst, said the legislation was intended to provide the Chinese Communist Party with a legal basis to seek assistance and cooperation from Western governments while projecting an image of governance based on the rule of law. He noted that Western democracies generally lack extradition treaties with Beijing and frequently reject its requests for assistance in apprehending suspects because of concerns over China's lack of judicial transparency, political persecution of dissidents and religious believers, the death penalty, torture and other human rights violations. Wang Dan, a prominent Chinese dissident living in exile in Taiwan and a leader of the 1989 student democracy movement, also expressed concern over the legislation during his YouTube talk show. Describing the law as putting "on a legal cloak" for controversial overseas operations, Wang Dan warned that its broad coverage of alleged cross-border corruption could allow Chinese law enforcement agencies to expand their interpretation of jurisdiction. He said Chinese authorities could potentially scrutinise financial transactions between overseas dissidents and their relatives or associates in China, identifying individuals connected to such transactions as persons of interest in corruption investigations. This, he warned, could turn economic investigations into instruments of pressure and create a chilling effect among dissidents. Heng He, a US-based senior China analyst and current affairs commentator, told The Epoch Times that Beijing had previously faced international criticism for allegedly kidnapping or apprehending individuals overseas and was now seeking new legislation to legitimise such operations. He pointed to previous overseas "persuasion to return" campaigns, which allegedly involved stalking, threats and pressure on family members in China to compel targeted individuals to return. "Now, the new law will make it easier for Beijing to frame such actions as anti-corruption law enforcement," Heng said. Meanwhile, a Chinese lawyer identified by the pseudonym Zhang Ting, citing fears of reprisals, questioned the effectiveness of the legislation in addressing corruption within the country. He argued that corruption in China stemmed from the absence of effective checks and balances on political power and could not be resolved simply by introducing another law. Describing the legislation as "a tool for political purges", Zhang said it represented an extension of the CCP's internal power struggles. Wang, He further argued that the party's anti-corruption campaigns were selective and largely influenced by officials' political loyalty to top leadership. According to him, political alignments and factional rivalries within the CCP remained significant factors in determining who faced investigations and who received protection. He warned that when targeting political rivals, Beijing could mobilise a wider range of government agencies to trace financial assets and seek assistance from foreign governments. The new legislation, Wang He said, could consequently become a legalised instrument for political power struggles under the guise of anti-corruption enforcement. (ANI)

(This story has not been edited by Devdiscourse staff and is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: Japan's household spending falls 6.8% in September despite rise in income
item.description: Japan's household spending declined by 6.8 per cent in September 2026 compared to the same month last year, even as household income increased, according to official data released by the Statistics ...
item.content:encoded:
Japan's household spending falls 6.8% in September despite rise in income Japan's household spending declined by 6.8 per cent in September 2026 compared to the same month last year, even as household income increased, according to official data released by the Statistics Bureau of Japan on Tuesday. ANI | Updated: 10-11-2026 15:45 IST | Created: 10-11-2026 15:45 IST

Representative image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Japan's household spending declined by 6.8 per cent in September 2026 compared to the same month last year, even as household income increased, according to official data released by the Statistics Bureau of Japan on Tuesday. The latest Family Income and Expenditure Survey, released by Japan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, showed that average monthly consumption expenditure among households with two or more people stood at 289,536 yen (USD 1,833). The bureau said consumption expenditure was "down 4.5% in nominal terms and down 6.8% in real terms from the previous year." The decline marked the tenth consecutive month of falling household spending in real terms, indicating continued weakness in consumption. The fall in spending also deepened from August, when household expenditure had declined by 3.1 per cent year-on-year in real terms. On a month-on-month basis, household spending fell by 2.8 per cent in September after seasonal adjustment, compared with a marginal increase of 0.1 per cent in August. The detailed survey data showed that several major spending categories registered declines during September. Spending on education fell 23.5 per cent in real terms, while expenditure on transport and communication declined 9.1 per cent. Expenditure on fuel, light and water charges dropped 10.5 per cent, while spending on culture and recreation declined 8.7 per cent. Food expenditure also fell 2.5 per cent in real terms compared with September last year. However, household income increased during the month, contrasting with the decline in consumption. According to the survey, average monthly income among workers' households with two or more people stood at 528,074 yen (USD 3,343). The Statistics Bureau said household income was "up 3.4% in nominal terms and up 0.9% in real terms from the previous year." The figures showed that consumer spending continued to decline in September despite an improvement in inflation-adjusted income among workers' households. (ANI)

FAST

LONDON, Nov 10 : Oil prices extended losses from the previous session on Tuesday after US President Donald Trump downplayed the need for additional military action against Iran, easing fears of sustained Middle East supply disruptions, with prospects of oversupply also in focus. Brent crude futures were down $2.39, or 2.58 per cent at $90.18 a barrel by 0930 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures fell $2.11, or 2.43 per cent to $84.74.  The Brent benchmark dropped below $90 on Tuesday for the first time since August 31, having settled down 5.85 per cent in the previous session. Trump said on Monday that he plans to hold off from new military strikes against Iran after appeals from countries in the region, including from Qatar's prime minister.

"The market continues to prioritise President Trump's more conciliatory tone toward Iran since the midterms," said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade. "While attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz are still occurring, they have not escalated in a way that has forced a fresh risk premium into the market."  In the physical crude oil market, the dated Brent benchmark, against which roughly two thirds of oil supply is priced, has weakened in recent weeks. The global oil market is showing signs of a return to excess supply as demand drops because of high prices, some analysts said. The global surplus is estimated at around 1.4 million barrels per day in October, JPMorgan said in a report last week. On the supply side, OPEC oil output rose in October, a Reuters survey found, led by gains in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq despite continued constraints on exports.    Brent has retreated about 23 per cent from the six-month high of $118 it touched on October 30 as fears that Trump might step up attacks on Iran after the US midterms have eased, though concerns remain over potential shipping disruption. Elsewhere, Russian and Ukrainian officials planned to meet on Tuesday for US-brokered talks — their first since February — after Trump suggested last week that a broad peace deal was possible after four and a half years of conflict.

Source: Reuters

HONG KONG, Nov 10 : Chinese chip companies Suzhou Denglin Technology and Jiangsu Xinde Semiconductor Technology ended their Hong Kong market debuts mixed on Tuesday after raising a combined HK$2.36 billion ($301 million) in initial public offerings. • AI chip designer Denglin opened at HK$229, 0.9 per cent below its offer price of HK$231, and closed at HK$213. Semiconductor packaging firm Xinde opened 20.5 per cent above its offer price of HK$8.88 at HK$10.70 and ended at HK$11.40 • Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index rose 0.44 per cent, while the Hang Seng Tech Index was up 1.08 per cent • Denglin raised HK$1.41 billion after pricing its offering at the bottom of the marketed range. Its retail tranche was 2.11 times subscribed, while the international tranche was 1.34 times covered

Its retail tranche was 9.84 times subscribed and the international offering was 1.13 times covered • Xinde provides chip packaging and testing services, and plans to use most of the proceeds to expand production capacity and develop advanced packaging technology ($1 = 7.8401 Hong Kong dollars)

item.title: US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review
item.description: The United States is set to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the UN's top rights body since it was created two decades ago.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review

US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review Trump administration declines to participate in the UN Human Rights Council's Universal Periodic Review, which examines the rights records of all 193 member states every four to five years

The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago | Image: Bloomberg

AP Geneva 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 10 2026 | 2:47 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The United States is set to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the UN's top rights body since it was created two decades ago. The Trump administration last year pulled the US out of the Human Rights Council, accusing it of an anti-US and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn't uphold the very values it promotes. Supporters back the council's mandate to keep tabs on human rights in all UN member states including the US, which has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific - which the administration has said are designed to protect US workers and help keep the country safe.

The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 UN member states - generally about every four to five years - as part of a process known as the universal periodic review. The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the US government might change its mind. Also Read

Meet Nithya Raman, the India-born politician who won LA mayoral race

US AI data centres turn to retired jet engines to meet power demand

Private jet carrying 9 crashes near Trump's Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida

It did not. "(W)e give no credibility to the agency," a State Department spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press. "This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own values' as it pushes anti-American rhetoric," the spokesperson said, alleging the council's "persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators."   The council says the process requires participation of the country in question, and in the case of an absence of any national representatives, the review cannot go forward.

As part of such reviews, national delegations - which at times can include a dozen officials or more - make a presentation, face questions and hear recommendations from other national envoys. It's supposed to be a sweeping and constructive process, akin to holding up a mirror to governments to improve their human rights policies. Critics of the US snub warn that the walkout could encourage other countries - many of which bristle about intense scrutiny from human rights monitors - to follow suit. Jamil Dakwar, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's human rights program, said: "The administration is saying to the world, we don't care about whether you would review us or not, we're going to continue to violate human rights unabashed'."   "And we are saying: No, enough is enough. This council should hold the United States accountable'," he told reporters Monday in Geneva, as part of a push by civil society to raise awareness about the US rights record.

He said the ACLU and allies have called on the UN human rights chief to respond by presenting an update on rights in the United States early next year. Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute who was the council's first secretary, said the US walkout could affect the credibility of the council's review system. "If the predominant global power - which has always claimed to adhere to the human rights norms - doesn't show up and doesn't even justify why, then you are in big trouble," he said.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: Pentagon chief Hegseth expected to face House impeachment vote this week
item.description: Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass but conviction appears unlikely.
item.dc:creator: CNA

Pentagon chief Hegseth expected to face House impeachment vote this week

Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass but conviction appears unlikely.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks during an event at Sparrows Point Shipyard, in Baltimore County, Maryland, US, Oct 6, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Eric Lee)

10 Nov 2026 06:33AM (Updated: 10 Nov 2026 12:51PM)

FAST

WASHINGTON: Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, calls himself the secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and "woke" when he took office last year. Now, with an expected House impeachment vote this week, he could soon share something in common with an actual secretary of war. William Belknap, who held that title in 1876, became the first, and to date only, civilian leader of the US military to be impeached by Congress. US Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced eight articles of impeachment on Monday (Nov 9), setting off a two-day clock for a potential House vote on charges including waging war against Iran without congressional approval and other abuses of power. Massie, addressing reporters, cautioned that Republican leadership could try to avoid a straight vote on impeachment by trying to dismiss it with a procedural motion.

"They may try to get out of an actual vote on the substance of this. We should have a vote and a rigorous debate on these eight articles of impeachment," he told a press conference. Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass even with President Donald Trump’s Republicans still controlling the House until Democrats take over on Jan 3. Conviction appears unlikely in the Senate, however, where a two-thirds majority is required and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats. US President Donald Trump, in an interview with Reuters on Monday, strongly defended Hegseth, pointing to the US military's performance in Iran and Venezuela: "Well, he won two wars. I don't know how you can impeach him." House Speaker Mike Johnson opposed the effort, saying impeachment “in the middle of hostilities abroad” would be “a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see”. Voter anger over the war helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week's midterm elections , intensifying Republican divisions over a conflict that Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned and Hegseth has defended as “courageous and historic”. Accused of taking huge kickbacks, Belknap handed President Ulysses Grant his resignation ahead of his scheduled impeachment vote and, according to a Senate history, “burst into tears”. The House impeached him anyway, but the Senate later acquitted him after falling short of the required two-thirds majority. By contrast, Hegseth is promising to stay and fight.

HEGSETH SAYS HE IS NOT WORRIED Hegseth has mounted a social media campaign, saying in a defiant video message last week that he would not back down. He also drew a comparison to Trump, who was impeached twice, saying: "It didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me." Asked if he had enough Republican support to defeat the impeachment push, Hegseth said on Monday: "We're not worried about that." He announced a Tuesday press conference, his first at the Pentagon since May. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also White House national security adviser, called the impeachment push "unfair," telling reporters: "I think Pete's done a good job. I really do."

Related:

Trump revives election fraud claims after crushing midterm defeat

Republicans call for Trump to change course after midterm drubbing

Trump, speaking with Reuters, extolled Hegseth's performance in the Iran war, which is at an impasse, and with Venezuela, where the US military deposed that country's president, Nicolás Maduro, in a surprise January commando raid on his compound in the Venezuelan capital. "Well, what about impeaching the people from Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq and all of that, where we fought forever and nothing happened?" Trump asked. DEFENCE SPENDING AT RISK? Some Republican lawmakers have expressed concern that if Hegseth stays, his strained relationship with Congress will undermine the Trump administration's push for a US$1.5 trillion defence spending package. Massie, a Trump critic who is leaving office in January, warned in a statement on Monday that impeachment would be "much gentler" than what's in store for Hegseth once Democrats take control in January. "They will hold hearings and trials. President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate," Massie said. Democrats have promised to investigate Hegseth over issues including the firing of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and other senior leaders. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Sunday he was a "hard yes" on a measure to impeach Hegseth. US Senator Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who is expected to become majority leader, said on Monday the Senate needs to put Hegseth on trial. "Hegseth waged this war illegally, in open defiance of the Constitution and multiple War Powers Resolutions this Congress passed to end the fighting," he said. Massie's articles of impeachment accuse Hegseth of "high crimes and misdemeanours" ranging from waging the Iran war to various alleged abuses of power, including violating the free speech rights of US Senator Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat. Last year, Hegseth sought to prosecute Kelly after he and five other Democrats in Congress with backgrounds in the military and intelligence urged US troops to refuse illegal orders. Hegseth accused them of sedition, something Trump at the time said in a social media post was "punishable by DEATH!"

item.title: A new deal brings together two long-life Canadian oilsands and heavy oil companies
item.description: Strathcona Resources Ltd. has signed a deal to buy Greenfire Resources Ltd. in a deal valued at up to $2.9 billion, including debt.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: CALGARY — Strathcona Resources Ltd. has signed a deal to buy Greenfire Resources Ltd. in a deal valued at up to $2.9 billion, including debt. The company says the deal will bring together two long-life oilsands and heavy oil companies. Strathcona says it expects the existing Greenfire leadership team to continue to lead day-to-day operations for the Greenfire assets within a new Strathcona business unit. Under the agreement, Greenfire shareholders may choose to receive either 0.25 of a Strathcona share or $11 in cash for each Greenfire share they hold. Strathcona shares closed at $36.34 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Friday, while Greenfire shares closed at :$7.93. Strathcona says the Waterous Energy Fund, which holds 72 per cent of Greenfire’s outstanding shares and a 57 per cent stake in Strathcona, has agreed to support the deal and plans to take its payment in shares. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

item.title: Blast at steel plant kills 16 in Turkey
item.description: Another 13 people were injured following the blast, and 10 others are still waiting to be rescued.
item.dc:creator: Marina Meireles
item.content:encoded:
Blast at steel plant kills 16 in Turkey

Marina Meireles | November 9, 2026 | 1:01 pm News   Europe   Iron Ore

Stock image.

A blast at a steel and iron plant in western Turkey killed 16 people on Nov. 9, with search and rescue operations still ongoing to reach 10 people still trapped under the rubble, President Tayyip Erdogan said.

The explosion happened around noon local time, at the Habas Demir Celik facility in the Aliaga district of Turkey’s Izmir province, where iron and steel are processed.

The incident occured when a ceiling crane snapped and fell into an arc furnace during the molten steel casting process.

13 people were injured, and 2 were in serious condition, Bloomberg reported. The victims were transported to different hospitals in the region.

The government said the incident is under investigation.

(With files from Reuters and Bloomberg)

item.title: Copper price bounces after worst week since March amid scramble for metal in China
item.description: The Yangshan premium for copper shipped into China climbed to a record $230 a tonne on Monday, spot premiums in Shanghai have tripled in two weeks, and deliverable stocks on the SHFE would cover less than a day of Chinese consumption.
item.dc:creator: Frik Els
item.content:encoded:
Copper price bounces after worst week since March amid scramble for metal in China

Staff Writer | November 9, 2026 | 12:39 pm Markets   China   United States   Copper

Copper cathode production in electrowinning plant. ( Stock image by Jorge. )

Copper prices rebounded on Monday, recovering part of last week’s steep losses as risk appetite steadied, the dollar slipped and tight physical supply in China came back into focus.

Comex copper for December delivery, the most active contract in New York, was trading at $6.3550 a pound ($14,010 a tonne) late morning in New York, up 1.9% on the day and roughly 13% higher so far in 2026.

On the London Metal Exchange, three-month copper rose 0.9% to $13,890 a tonne by mid-afternoon in London, having lost 2.7% last week in its steepest weekly decline since March. In Shanghai the most-traded contract gained 0.5% to 107,430 yuan ($16,096) a tonne.

China squeeze

“Copper is recovering as risk sentiment stabilises and tight physical supply in China returns to focus,” ING commodities strategist Ewa Manthey told Reuters, adding that the rise in spot premiums shows metal remains difficult to secure.

The Yangshan copper premium, which reflects demand for metal imported into the top consumer, rose to a record $230 a tonne on Monday. Copper stocks in Shanghai Futures Exchange-monitored warehouses fell more than 24% last week to 33,848 tonnes, the lowest in almost three years, according to John Gross of The Copper Journal . That would cover China’s copper consumption for less than a day.

Bloomberg reports the Singapore-based trader Trafigura, one of the biggest in the copper market, has over the past two weeks approached several producers and traders in Asia seeking to buy large volumes over November and December, and has been willing to outbid rivals to secure cargoes.

Spot premiums in Shanghai have tripled over the past two weeks to a record 2,615 yuan ($392) a tonne, according to Shanghai Metals Market, while premiums for imported copper tracked by Fastmarkets have jumped more than 40% to $195–210 a tonne, the highest in data going back to 2017. On the SHFE, the spread between December and January contracts blew out to more than 1,200 yuan a tonne late on Friday, the widest backwardation since 2005.

Chinese smelters are struggling to source concentrate and scrap, and a crackdown on illegal mining in the Democratic Republic of Congo – China’s biggest source of refined copper – in which the government seized more than 500 trucks and several thousand tonnes of copper and cobalt, threatens to crimp supplies further.

“One of the main drivers for the tightness is the slowdown in refined production growth, which reflects the fact that smelters have been struggling for feedstock,” Morgan Stanley metals strategist Amy Gower told Bloomberg. “The demand indicators are fairly lackluster, so it does point to supply issues being the cause of the tightness in the Chinese market.”

Ship to shore

Comex depots hold 732,943 tonnes, more than double a year ago, after two years in which miners and traders prioritised shipments to the US ahead of threatened import tariffs.

On paper, the surge in Shanghai premiums and spreads is now large enough to cover the cost of shipping copper from the US back to China. The hindrance, people familiar with the trade told Bloomberg, is that those cargoes would be worth far more in the US if tariffs are eventually imposed.

“This is starting to become more of a question, but for it to happen I think you’d need tariffs to be definitively ruled out,” Gower said. “Our base case is that the US material will be quite sticky and will only get drawn down through under-importing.”

Temporary gains?

Monday’s bounce may not hold. “Today’s move does not necessarily mark the end of the correction,” ING’s Manthey said. “Prices remain vulnerable to further weakness if broader market sentiment deteriorates again.”

A Democratic sweep in last week’s US midterm elections has reduced the prospects for the Trump administration’s planned tariffs on refined copper and raised the odds of tighter restrictions on data centres, threatening both the AI-related demand and the tariff-driven stockpiling that have supported prices this year. TD Securities said on Friday that copper faces a further slide as the result weakens expectations for import tariffs.

Last week also offered a partial answer to the question of how much of copper’s 2026 rally rests on AI hype rather than fundamentals. Gross says: the metal fell in lockstep with tech stocks. The physical demand story has not changed – US construction spending on data centres hit a record annualized $96.5 billion in September, according to The Copper Journal – but a “not in my backyard” contingent emboldened by the election could see that spending stall too.

Citi struck a similar note on Monday: “While low visible inventories and elevated geopolitical risks should continue to provide downside support in the near-term, the outlook for next year remains challenged by Indonesian-led supply growth and a muted demand environment.”

Miners rebound

Copper producers rallied with the metal on Monday. Freeport-McMoRan climbed 5.8% in early afternoon trade in New York, lifting its market value to $90.2 billion, less than a week after its board approved a $4.5 billion expansion of the Bagdad mine in Arizona that would more than double the operation’s copper output to over 400 million pounds a year from mid-2030 and make it the second-largest copper mine in the US.

Southern Copper added 6.0% to $151.3 billion and Teck Resources rose 5.9% to $31.4 billion. BHP gained 3.2% to $207.4 billion, Rio Tinto 3.0% to $147.8 billion and Glencore 5.3% to $81.7 billion. Anglo American was up 6.2% and Antofagasta 6.7% in US trading, with Lundin Mining up 6.5% and First Quantum Minerals 5.2% in Toronto.

Ivanhoe Mines added 3.5%, but the Vancouver-based company is still down 47% this year after a second production downgrade at its Kamoa-Kakula complex in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The bounce follows a brutal October. The MINING.COM TOP 50 ranking of the world’s most valuable miners lost $226 billion last month on top of September’s $264 billion decline, and is now $712 billion below its February peak.

In project news, Rio Tinto is injecting $144 million into Resolution Copper in Arizona after a land-swap court victory, a project JPMorgan says is central to its view that US copper output could more than double . In Chile, Codelco and Pucobre have cleared a key hurdle for an $870 million copper mine slated to begin construction in 2027, even as the state miner contends with an inflated output scandal that has grown to 42,100 tonnes.

item.title: Everything Jensen Huang Said About China Is Out the Window
item.description: No American argued harder for selling artificial-intelligence chips to China than Nvidia Corp.’s chief executive, Jensen Huang. item.title: Trump says Qatar, Saudi prefer peace in Iran conflict
item.description: "The United States of America is fully locked and loaded with the best equipment ever made, and we don't think there's going to be any reason to use it," said Trump.
item.dc:creator: CNA
item.content:encoded:

World

Trump says Qatar, Saudi prefer peace in Iran conflict

"The United States of America is fully locked and loaded with the best equipment ever made, and we don't think there's going to be any reason to use it," said Trump.

US President Donald Trump speaks during a rally at Guardian Centres in Perry, Georgia, US, Oct 24, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Umit Bektas)

FAST

WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said on Monday (Nov 9) he plans to hold off on new military strikes against Iran for the time being after appeals from countries in the region, including from Qatar's prime minister in White House talks. Trump, in a Reuters interview and a later appearance in the White House press briefing room, said he plans to keep up a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz for now. "The United States of America is fully locked and loaded with the best equipment ever made, and we don't think there's going to be any reason to use it," Trump told reporters. He said he was acting "at the behest of countries that are their neighbours" and specifically cited Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait and others that prefer the US not launch new attacks.

Trump spoke after meeting with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, a key intermediary with Tehran, as efforts to end the war ramp up following last week's US midterm election. More than eight months into the conflict he launched alongside Israel on Feb 28, Trump has played down the likelihood of major warfare restarting soon but remains unwilling to accept an existing Iranian truce plan. Senior US and Gulf officials have cast doubt on the chances of an imminent deal. Mutual attacks continue, with the US striking Iran's Qeshm island overnight, according to Iranian state media, and Iran attacking tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz this month while its Yemeni Houthi allies have hit Saudi Arabia.

DIPLOMATIC MOVES Al-Thani, who is both prime minister and foreign minister of Qatar, met Trump after visiting Tehran last week. The prime minister called his talks with both Trump and Vice President JD Vance positive. "Grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region," he said on X. Iranian security council chief Mohsen Rezaei said on X the US should "stop manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks" and that it was "time to surrender to the seven conditions Iran has repeatedly set out". Iran's proposal to end the war involves an end to the US blockade of its ports, the lifting of some sanctions and a halt to bombing in return for Tehran stopping its own blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, with talks on its nuclear programme and other sanctions to follow. The US has repeatedly rejected that plan, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio describing Tehran's conditions on Sunday as "outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic". Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei defended the plan on Monday as the most reasonable offer on the table. Senior US Republicans including Vice President JD Vance have blamed their party's losses in last week's elections on the Iran war. Despite the growing domestic political pressure to end the conflict, Rubio said he did not believe a diplomatic breakthrough was imminent. A senior United Arab Emirates official, Anwar Gargash, echoed that view on Monday, saying a comprehensive political settlement between the US and Iran appeared difficult. "We should ... prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional order can be taken for granted," he said. Vance, who led the negotiations for a short-lived truce in June, will also meet Al-Thani, whose country has been a prime mediator since early in the war, conveying messages between the sides and proposing ways to bridge their differences.

Related:

Trump says he is highly unlikely to order Iran strikes if talks progress

Iran says forces 'stronger' than at beginning of war

Anxiety over the war has pervaded the region for months, and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said on Monday he had told Trump that Ankara did not want to see a new escalation. "We emphasise at every opportunity that it is possible to resolve these issues through dialogue and diplomacy. Unfortunately, we see a negative shift once again. We are doing our utmost to prevent this," Erdogan told reporters. MILITARY ACTION Sunday night's strikes on Qeshm island did not impact vital infrastructure or services, a provincial official told Iran's semi-official Fars news agency on Monday. The US has not commented on the Iranian media reports. A senior Iranian source told Reuters that US strikes were targeting Iranian radar systems serving both air defence and ship navigation, as well as bases for missile launchers and mine-laying systems. Attacks on tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz ramped up sharply in October and have continued at the highest rate since the start of the war, figures from international maritime agencies showed last week. Iran, which typically does not acknowledge striking vessels that report being hit by projectiles, said on Sunday a tanker had hit a mine east of the Strait of Hormuz. A state television reporter said on Monday that 11 tankers had been "disabled" over the past 10 days.

Source: Reuters/fs/fh

item.title: Brazil picks 27 critical minerals in push for local supply chain
item.description: New classification will steer public funding toward domestic processing and projects considered vital to industrial growth.
item.dc:creator: Marina Meireles
item.content:encoded:
Brazil picks 27 critical minerals in push for local supply chain

Marina Meireles | November 8, 2026 | 11:37 am Critical Minerals   Exploration   Regulatory Issues   Latin America   Aluminum   Chrome   Cobalt   Copper   Gold   Graphite   Iron Ore   Lithium   Manganese   Molybdenum   Nickel   Palladium   Platinum   Rare Earth   Tin   Tungsten   Uranium   Vanadium   Zinc

Caldeira rare earth project location. ( Image courtesy of Meteoric Resources | Facebook. )

Brazil has designated 27 critical minerals as the country looks to accelerate mineral projects, develop the sector domestically and reduce its reliance on exporting raw materials.

The National Council for Industrialization of Critical and Strategic Minerals (CIMCE) approved the list on Nov. 5, dividing the minerals into three priority groups based on their importance to national security, industrial development and supply chain resilience. The classification will help determine which mining projects qualify for federal support.

“For so long we have exported mineral wealth as ore and imported it back as a finished product, developing value and jobs in other countries,” development, industry, commerce and services minister, Brazil’s minister of development, industry, commerce and services, Márcio Elias Rosa, said. “We want to stop this cycle and create a strategy to develop this here.”

The initiative comes as countries seek to diversify supplies of minerals essential to electric vehicles, renewable energy, defence and advanced technologies.

Brazil hopes to capture more value from its mineral resources by encouraging investment in refining and manufacturing rather than relying primarily on raw material exports.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said the government intends to work with international partners rather than control the industry outright.

“We don’t want the state to have absolute control over exploration, processing and industrialization,” Lula said during the council meeting, Bloomberg reported. “We need to work with other countries that want to join us in developing and processing this wealth.”

Only the 27 minerals included in the list, and nationally registered projects, will be eligible to receive government support, according to the new government strategy.

The list

The council identified nine high-priority minerals: rare earths, graphite, lithium, nickel, cobalt, copper, manganese, silicon and uranium. The government said high-priority minerals have a high geopolitical risk, global demand and low substitution rate for other materials, CNN Brasil reported .

“The list will function as the compass of Brazilian mineral politics, giving the sector the most important tool: predictability,” the mines and energy ministry said in a statement to G1.

Eight minerals fall into the medium-priority category: tungsten, chrome, vanadium, tantalum, titanium, phosphate, potassium and sulfur. The remaining 10 are classified as lower priority: niobium, tin, iron, zinc, gold, magnesium, molybdenum, thorium, aluminum and platinum group metals.

The classifications will undergo reviews every four years to account for economic, technological and geopolitical developments.

Investment priority

Having this list will allow the government to direct financing toward projects that strengthen domestic mineral production and processing. The rules for approval or denial of projects still need to be defined.

The council also created a fund to reduce risks and expand investments in the sector, known as FGAM. It can receive up to R$2 billion (about $364 million) from the federal government as well as more from local and state governments and private investment.

A separate Federal Program for Critical and Strategic Minerals (PFMCE) will have an annual funding limit of R$1 billion ($180 million) between 2030 and 2034 so companies can invest in mining development and transformation.

The measures follow Lula’s approval in September of R$5 billion (about $909 million) in funding to advance rare earths exploration, part of Brazil’s broader push to develop its mineral industry.

Lula’s Brazil win puts rare earths in Trump’s crosshairs

Both the council and government aim to have another meeting on this issue before the end of the year to better define supply chain priorities to advance investment decisions in the sector.

The list will be reassessed every four years and may undergo changes based on economical, technological or geopolitical changes across the globe.

(With files from Bloomberg)

item.title: Nasdaq dives 5.6% after Democrats’ win, VIX rises 70% on AI and Fed fears
item.description: Wall Street is preparing for a volatile start to Monday, November 9, following a sharp technology-led selloff, renewed US military actions in Iran, and heig
item.dc:creator: Cointurk
item.content:encoded: Wall Street is preparing for a volatile start to Monday, November 9, following a sharp technology-led selloff, renewed US military actions in Iran, and heightened speculation about another Federal Reserve rate hike. Despite warnings from some market observers about a potential “Black Monday” crash, evidence of an imminent collapse remains limited. Tech stocks tumble after Democrats take Congress Volatility spikes as VIX soars but crash remains unconfirmed Geopolitical pressure and Fed expectations fuel uncertainty Tech stocks tumble after Democrats take Congress The Nasdaq Composite plummeted 5.56% on November 5, as investors reevaluated technology sector prospects after the Democratic Party secured control of Congress in the US midterm elections. This shift has fueled concerns over stricter regulations related to artificial intelligence and increased operational costs for data centers, raising doubts about the pace of future infrastructure development. Reuters reported that the S&P 500 declined about 4.4% the same day, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed more than 1,800 points. The initial optimism following Wednesday’s market rally quickly vanished, replaced by fears that legislative changes could limit growth in AI and related industries. In the credit markets, traders sought higher yields for corporate bonds issued by AI-focused companies. While this trend highlights tighter lending conditions, it does not necessarily point to widespread capital flight from the sector. Mini dictionary: S&P 500 is a major US stock market index composed of 500 leading publicly traded companies, often considered a primary benchmark for the overall US equity market. The sharp Nasdaq drop reflected growing unease over government oversight and rising costs in the artificial intelligence sector following Democratic gains in Congress. Index Change (%) Result Nasdaq Composite -5.56% Major decline S&P 500 -4.4% Significant drop Dow Jones -1,800 pts Steep fall Volatility spikes as VIX soars but crash remains unconfirmed The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX), often called Wall Street’s “fear gauge,” jumped nearly 70% on November 5, climbing from 16.61 to 28.18. This move marked the third-largest single-day percentage increase since 1990, though the VIX stayed below crisis-era extremes. By Friday, the VIX moderated to 25.64 as semiconductor stocks contributed to a partial rebound. The Nasdaq recovered 1.1% and the S&P 500 edged up 0.3%, but both benchmarks ended the week with overall losses, reflecting lingering market anxiety. Analysts cautioned that the late recovery did not eliminate the risk of renewed selling. Friday’s recovery provided some relief after Thursday’s steep losses, yet continuing volatility left investors wary ahead of Monday’s trading session. Geopolitical pressure and Fed expectations fuel uncertainty Tensions increased after US President Donald Trump confirmed targeted strikes against Iranian air defense installations on Qeshm Island. This action followed previous US military operations amid the ongoing conflict with Iran. Rising concerns over the security of the Strait of Hormuz continued to affect global risk sentiment and oil markets. The US labor market report released on Friday showed that American employers added 165,000 jobs in October, well above expectations of 65,000. Unemployment fell to 4.1%. Futures pricing suggested a 78% chance that the Federal Reserve would raise rates in December, intensifying pressure on technology companies that rely on low-cost financing. Higher borrowing expenses threaten to squeeze profits for heavily leveraged tech firms and data center operators. The outlook for Monday’s market open remains highly uncertain, as investors grapple with unresolved geopolitical tensions and ongoing economic policy debates. While risks have risen, current data do not confirm a repeat of previous “Black Monday” style crashes. Mini dictionary: The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) tracks market expectations of near-term volatility based on S&P 500 index options. Higher values indicate rising uncertainty and increased risk aversion among traders.

item.title: Ontario’s Lecce warns that Democrats offer no tariff cure
item.description: Canada shouldn’t expect the United States to lift tariffs simply because Democrats won control of Congress, Ontario Energy and Mines Minister said.
item.dc:creator: Northern Miner Staff
item.content:encoded:
Ontario’s Lecce warns that Democrats offer no tariff cure

Frédéric Tomesco | November 5, 2026 | 4:00 pm Regulatory Issues   Canada   USA   Aluminum   Copper   Nickel

Ontario Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce (in a file photo) says Canada still faces U.S. protectionism regardless of the midterm elections. Credit: The Northern Miner

Canada shouldn’t expect the United States to lift tariffs simply because Democrats won control of Congress , Ontario Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce said.

Speaking two days after the U.S. midterm elections, Lecce said the outcome could strengthen Prime Minister Mark Carney’s negotiating position. Still, protectionism runs through both major U.S. political parties, which will leave Canadian exporters exposed even after President Donald Trump leaves office, he cautioned.

“I’m just not convinced it materially changes our fundamental reality on the ground,” Lecce said of the U.S. midterm election results in a lunchtime speech Thursday to the Empire Club of Toronto. “The change of the composition of Congress doesn’t change the policy position of America vis-a-vis tariffs.”

Lecce’s remarks underscore the gap between securing a trade agreement and eliminating tariffs. For Canadian metals producers, a trade deal may offer greater certainty without removing the tariffs that raise the cost of selling into the U.S. market.

Lame-duck Trump

Democrats won both the House of Representatives and Senate in Tuesday’s elections, giving them power to challenge Trump’s agenda when the new Congress convenes in January. The results leave the Republican president facing an opposition-controlled Congress for his final two years in office.

While U.S. political analysts pointed to voter frustration over high prices, the Iran war and government corruption as key factors behind Tuesday’s outcome, Lecce insists trade friction with Canada figured prominently in the campaign.

“Tariffs were on the ballot,” he said. “We stayed in our lane, but it’s clear that Canada was on the ballot.”

New momentum

Negotiations between the neighbours and trading partners have been showing fresh momentum. Carney said Tuesday that Washington had dropped demands affecting Canada’s ability to negotiate agreements with other countries. Trump, meanwhile, said a deal was close, Reuters reported.

Carney’s recent comments on the state of talks are “a good signal,” Lecce said. The Democrats’ win Tuesday “perhaps will enable a better hand for Prime Minister Carney and the national government to land a deal.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford should get credit for pressing Carney to reject an earlier agreement that would have entrenched tariffs, Lecce added.

Recounting a conversation between the two leaders, Lecce said Ford told Carney this summer: “’Do not sign a bad deal that will lock us and create the precedent of acceptance of tariffs in perpetuity. No deal is materially better than a good deal.”

Ford also made it clear to Carney that Ontario would oppose the deal publicly, according to Lecce.

Wider dispute

Ottawa suspended negotiations with the U.S. in August. Washington subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on $27.6 billion of Canadian goods, prompting Canadian countermeasures .

The dispute extends beyond those measures. According to Canada’s Trade Commissioner Service, U.S. sectoral tariffs on covered steel, aluminum and copper products range from 15% to 50%, subject to product and content rules. Certain other tariffs apply even when Canadian goods qualify for preferential treatment under the continental trade agreement.

The bilateral talks are unfolding alongside negotiations over the Canada–United States–Mexico Agreement, or CUSMA. The pact replaced the North American Free Trade Agreement in July 2020, following renegotiation during Trump’s first presidency.

Washington declined to extend CUSMA in its current form at the July 1 review. That triggered annual reviews rather than immediate expiry: the agreement’s existing term runs to 2036, and the three countries can jointly approve another 16-year term.

Canada has explicitly linked those discussions to relief from sectoral tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber. Preserving CUSMA and resolving the tariff dispute therefore remain connected negotiating objectives.

Diversification

Even as efforts advance to rebuild the American relationship, Canada and Ontario should continue to deepen ties with other nations, Lecce argued.

“We should strengthen that relationship [with the U.S.], get it back on track, but be very vigorous in diversification,” he said. Ontario’s goal is “to make sure we are less exposed, less shocked by that vulnerability when conservatively, well over 75% of our trade is going to one nation.”

Even so, “it doesn’t mean that we can’t hope for some return to what I’d call just normal, respectful civil dialog with the most foundational relationship on earth, which is the United States.”

item.title: AngloGold plans $900 million mine expansion amid stronger profit
item.description: The investment comes as the gold miner aims to incrementally increase production by the end of the decade.
item.dc:creator: Marina Meireles
item.content:encoded:
AngloGold plans $900 million mine expansion amid stronger profit

Marina Meireles | November 5, 2026 | 9:55 am Top Companies   Africa   Latin America   Gold

Geita open pit mine, located in northwestern Tanzania, is AngloGold’s largest single gold mining operation. ( Image: AngloGold Ashanti )

AngloGold Ashanti (NYSE: AU) plans to invest up to $900 million in expanding brownfield operations across its portfolio, targeting a production increase of 300,000 ounces to 450,000 ounces by 2030.

The investments will focus on the Geita gold mine in Tanzania, Siguiri in Guinea and Cuiabá in Brazil, as well as the ongoing ramp-up at Obuasi in Ghana. The company expects the projects to generate real internal rates of return exceeding 35%, Reuters reported.

“These are high-return, capital efficient projects at our operating mines that are expected to provide high-margin ounces and unlock further value from our portfolio,” AngloGold Ashanti CEO Alberto Calderon said in a statement.

The plan is to use existing infrastructure and operational footprints to reduce risk and optimize capital intensity.

Geita will receive the larger portion of the funding, up to $580 million to raise output to 600,000 ounces by 2030. Cuiabá’s expansion will cost between $200 million and $250 million, adding about 75,000 ounces to its output.

Another $70 million will be put towards the Suguiri mine, looking to add another 100,000 ounces to its production.

Shares in AngloGold Ashanti were up 0.35% to $88.22 apiece by mid-day Thursday in New York, valuing the company at $44.6 billion.

Profit on the rise

AngloGold reported a 12% increase for its EBITDA for Q3 2026 to $1,568 million, from $1,400 million for Q3 2025.

The company said on its Q3 earnings release that the growth is supported by the increase in the average gold price received per ounce to $4,239/oz, from $3,490/oz in the same period in 2025.

AngloGold Ashanti said its full year gold production guidance of 2,800,000 ounces to 3,170,000 ounces is reaffirmed.

Its gold production was about 3.65% more costly than the previous quarter, at $1,534 per ounce due gold royalties and higher fuel costs.

The company also reported that a worker died due to a rockfall at the Sukari underground mine in August 2026. Operations were suspended while investigations took place, but have since resumed.

(With files from Reuters)

item.title: テンセントがオラクルからAI半導体10万個をリース、70億ドル規模－FT
item.description:
（ブルームバーグ）： 中国のテンセント・ホールディングス（騰訊）は、東南アジアでオラクルから先端のAI半導体を借り受けることで合意した。テンセントにとってAI半導体のリース契約としては過去最大規模となる。英紙フィナンシャル・タイムズ（FT）が事情に詳しい関係者の話として報じた。
報道によると、テンセントは、5年間の契約の一環として10万個の半導体を利用できるようになる。契約額は70億ドル（約1兆1000億円）に上るという。
中国のAI開発企業は米国の輸出規制を回避するため、米エヌビディア製など中国国内では入手できないAIアクセラレーターを海外で借りて利用している。中国のテクノロジー企業は、東南アジアのデータセンターの最大顧客層の一つとなっている。
テンセントとオラクルの担当者は、ブルームバーグ・ニュースのコメント要請に直ちに応じなかった。
原題：Tencent Leases AI Chips From Oracle
